to everybody else for six months or
more, is about to undergo a rigid diag-
nosis to determine what kind of an op-
eration, if any, is necessary to restore
him to normal health and efficiency.

what surgeons call an exploratory op-
eration. Indeed, under the authori-

may do almost anything to the patient.
Congress and the general public
seem to be in much the same frame
of mind with respect to the coal indus-
try that was manifested by the har-
ried wife of a chronic invalid.
Sometimes,"" she said, ""I almost wish
he'd get well or—something!""
When anything gets wrong with
coal the whole economic and industrial
establishment is upset, and coal has
been ""ailing"" for a long time. The
condition became acute as a result of
the strike that began last April and
eventually Congress decided that some-
thing had to be done about it. Hence
the commission of experts with funds
of $500,000 to expend and a year's time
in which to make a thorough study to
determine what should be done with
coal.

in this case the patient itself is no
longer suffering, for the time being
at least, and whatever heroic remedies
are to be applied are for the benefit
of others. As soon as the strikes were
settled it was certain that all the min-
ers in both the bituminous and anthra-
cite fields would have steady employ-

mines have had everything their way,
while coal prices have been de-
termined largely on the basis of pro-
duction costs in mines that really
should not be open and these high-cost
mines have shown little if any profits.
So far as the miners are affected
the chief trouble has been irregular
and intermittent employment."

But first there floats into one's mind the old question: Were the allies right to grant an armistice at that particular moment in November, 1918? At the time I did not think so. I had just traversed the whole British war zone, and had seen that our troops were in high spirits and quite ready to go on. Clarence Martin had the misfortune to have his right wrist dislocated recently by having it caught in a pump jack at the Martin ranch at Mud Springs, New Mexico. He returned Wednesday from Lordsburg where he has been under the care of a physician, and is now on the road to recovery.
L. J. Owen and C. B. Nonemaker, manager of the Phelps Dodge Mercantile company stores at Morenci and Clifton respectively, were business visitors in the valley on Tuesday.
Mrs. Ethel Rainbolt was a visitor at Lordsburg for several days this week.
J. R. Jones, cashier of the Bank of Duncan, was business visitor at the county seat on Tuesday.
L. E. Wilkinson is drilling well at the Chiffon school at present.

Wm. Lewis went to Silver City on Monday where he was a witness in the Fulcher-Cranberry case. Mrs. J. E. Rayburn and Mr. and Mrs. J. S. White of the Steeplerock country were in Silver City this week, where they were called as witnesses in the Fulcher-Bradberry case. Mr. and Mrs. R. J. Coleman of Clifton were Duncan visitors on Tuesday. Mrs. Coleman will again teach in the Union High school during the coming year.

A protracted meeting is to be held at the Methodist church during the week and the meeting will take place outdoors. Miss Rosa Bouton, home demonstrator for Coconino, Apache and Navajo counties, who has been spending some time in the valley working with Miss R. S. Sinclair, home demonstrator for Greenlee county, has returned to her home. A number of interesting demonstrations were held during Miss Bouton's visit to the valley.
Mrs. J. R. Fowler and Mrs. J. A. Hunter have returned home after a ten days visit with friends at Lordsburg.
Mrs. C. M. Brooks was guest of Clifton relatives for a few days last week.
Mr. and Mrs. Joe Billingsley of Clifton were Duncan visitors on Monday.
Floyd Hightower, county supervisor, was at the county seat on Monday to attend regular meeting of the Board.
County Attorney Hooker was a visitor in the valley on last Friday.
Gerald Smith of Clifton is at present filling a position at the local flour mill.

Joe Whittredge, who has been seriously ill for some months, is now able to get about pretty freely. Mrs. S. L. Kemp and son, Ben, left on Monday morning for Palomas hot springs, New Mexico, where they will spend some time. Robt. E. Hancock was visiting with relatives at Lordsburg, for few days this week. Miss R. S. Sinclair home demonstrator for Greenlee county, was visitor at Morenci and Clifton on last Sunday.

Mr. and Mrs. Sam Tilley of Sheldon were Duncan visitors on Monday. Mrs. Frank Hyatt left on Tuesday morning for her home at Phoenix after spending a month with her parents, Mr. and Mrs. Robt. Sexton of Sheldon. Mrs. Mary Haynie recently went under an operation at the Lordsburg."

Henry C. Gay and family expect
to move down on the Umatilla river
where they have recently purchased
a tract of land from Walden Rhea.
This place is located a few miles be-
low the Pete Sheridan place at the
mouth of Butter creek and is ideally
situated for raising alfalfa, keeping
dairy cows, chickens and bees, and
Mr. Gay hopes to build up a good
home there. Mr. Rhea expects to
locate on a stock ranch.
